AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: The aim of this study was to observe the effect of sex on attaining optimal adherence to combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) longitudinally, while controlling for known adherence confounders: injection drug use (IDU) and ethnicity.

AbstractText.Label: DESIGN
AbstractText.content: Using the population-based HAART Observational Medical Evaluation and Research (HOMER) cohort, data were collected from HIV-positive adults, ≥19 years, receiving cART in British Columbia (BC), Canada, with data collected between 2000 and 2014. cART adherence was assessed using pharmacy refill data. The proportion of participants reaching optimal (≥95%) adherence by sex was compared per six-month period from initiation of therapy onwards. Generalized linear mixed models with logistic regression examined the effect of sex on cART adherence.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Among 4,534 individuals followed for a median of 65.9 months (interquartile range [IQR]: 37.0 to 103.2), 904 (19.9%) were women, 589 (13.0%) were Indigenous, and 1,603 (35.4%) had a history of IDU. A significantly lower proportion of women relative to men were optimally adherent overall (57.0% versus 77.1%; p < 0.001) and in covariate analyses. In adjusted analyses, female sex remained independently associated with suboptimal adherence overall (adjusted odds ratio [AOR]: 0.55; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.48 to 0.63).

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Women living with HIV had significantly lower cART adherence rates then men across a 14-year period overall, and by sub-group. Targeted research is required to identify barriers to adherence among women living with HIV in order to tailor women-centered HIV care and treatment support services.
